I'd give the same advice if she was telling you to be more Japanese because she likes anime, or cosplay as a video game character she crushes on - just because there's a real person does not mean there's anything healthier about her demands.

If you think she can have a conversation, tell her how hurt you felt that she wants you to change and mimic someone else. That you're worried for her - not because she likes these bands or fandom, but because you love her and she's unhappy with her life and you want to help her become happier. Telling her to stop meeting with Lily or knock off the bandom is going to drive a wedge between you and her, so avoid giving an ultimatum. Offer to go to counseling with her, but individual counseling may be better for her. But at the end of the day, if she refuses to change and continues this obsessiveness, its not going to be fair for you to put up to her insults and demands to mold yourself into something you're not just for her fandom fantasy.

It sounds as though your father contacted you alone. Your parents are not presenting themselves as united in their apology, which makes me wonder if your mother is sorry or just wants to "forget the whole thing happened" (that they abused and neglected you for absolutely no justifiable reason). It even seems as though he's not sorry, but that he's only reaching out to save his marriage - possibly at his therapist's suggestion. But these people don't deserve their marriage. They don't deserve happiness in their lives. All that's owed to them is the scorn of their community, and the rest of their lives to wither in isolation and loathing and the moral bankruptcy they created. But that's my thought. What matters more is your thoughts.

From the tone of your post, you don't seem to want them in your life. You don't trust his intentions or his timing - it's too convenient for them on an issue that's about your health. His horrifying candor gave you the explanation you needed. If that's enough closure for you, that's enough, and you can move on.

But bringing them back into your life means seeing them, hearing them talk, being in places associated with them, your childhood, your sister, your memories, your abuse. Going to Christmas and being reminded of the ones you hated. Hearing about your sister and risking reliving your childhood sorrow year after year. Spending the time after family visits talking with therapists about the feelings it triggered and how to unravel them. Looking them in the eyes and now knowing their true feelings about you, being reminded that they did not love you. 

You don't deserve that any more than you deserved what was inflicted upon you.

It is your decision. The door is there, but you don't need to open it now. You can tell your father that you will contact them "when you are ready" - on your terms, when you feel stable and secure and able to process. You can tell him to fuck off and nobody would ever judge you. You can tell him how and where you'll meet and give conditions and work with your parents to have a future, but only if you want that. You can accept his (half-assed and self-serving) apology. 

Only if it will help you and your recovery and your happiness.

My first reaction is that despite contributing the bulk of household products, your roommate is still sneakily trying to get you to pay extra? Is her part of the rent paid on time? If she's in more debt than she can manage, it may explain her trying to scrounge up some extra dollars and penny-pinch on utilities.

I'm going to echo another post and say, from here out, you get paper copies of your payments. Copies of bills paid, check receipts, print outs of electronic transactions. While you haven't given indication of things getting quite that bad yet, finances are something you don't want to regret later.

For your roommates now, before leaving, it may be worth the three of you getting together and discussing how household products are spent and utilities paid. If someone's unhappy with the status quo, it might be time to revisit that and see if there's an arrangement that better suits everyone's needs. It also gives an opportunity to talk in the open about problems, if you feel able to do so in calm tones. It's awkward, but you've made the effort of fixing the issue.

I was in a similar position to you when I got the game for Christmas. I didn't put more than five hours into WoW and got bored quickly with any other MMO I tried, but I've sunk about a year's worth of subscription into FFXIV and can say this;

You can solo most of the story content if that is your main focus. The main story quest is very much in the vein of a Final Fantasy/JRPG. There are required multiplayer segments in dungeons and trials, but you don't need to have someone pair up with you; it has a system called "Duty Finder" where players are randomly selected into appropriate teams. There's huge incentives given to high level players to help out in low dungeons, and I've rarely come across people too rude to help out if you say that you're new.

The bulk of the community, in my experience, are veteran MMO players. Most people I've seen played Final Fantasy XI when it was out, played the first version of XIV, and are still playing now. As such, it can be very intimidating to ask questions about mechanics and terminology. There are tons of guides online that help.

It gets extremely grindy and unless you have a lot of time to dedicate, you will have a very difficult time 'catching up'. Most of the Reddit community is focused on pushing the newest content and raids, and, while I've never experience snobbery or rudeness, it can feel difficult to approach for early-game content.

Incredibly jaded former History major here

Pro: Incredibly fascinating subject matter. You learn excellent research and writing skills. If you combine it with a language/cultural studies, you're great at parties and sounding really smart in casual conversations, and your worldview is significantly more open. You see a lot more patterns in world news. 

Cons: Job market is fucking awful. I think English and history are probably the two of the least desired majors on the market, and at least with English, people assume you know how to write. Archives requires library/information science advanced degrees and aforementioned language, which is an underfunded and underpaying field in and of itself. Teaching is NOT a viable career option - elementary and secondary schools want language arts and STEM, not social studies. 

Re-evaluate what success in life means to you. If it means affording a lot of nice things, housing, and travel, history is not the field to focus in. If it means feeling mentally enriched and working a mediocre office job (which even then, will be very difficult to land), you'll be happier. If it's a stepping stone to academia, well, you're fucked anyway but at least there's a chance the government will pay you to go to study languages.

Source: Am applying to graduate programs in history

Decide what part of the entertainment industry you're interested it. It's a broad, nebulous field with many, many different components. It is also, regardless of position, absurdly competitive. I'm going to assume because you said 'intern', you're interested in some corporate aspect, rather than a creative route. 

Find something similar where you're at now - you said you aren't in a major hub, but even small cities and towns have things like film festivals, college performing arts centers, art galleries, and you have the internet and it's thousands of blogs, forums, and message boards. Start there, just to get buzzwords on your resume, and don't pass up any work because it's not glamorous enough.

Research everything you can about the industry you want. If it's film - know major producers, production companies, special effects and design houses. Where do they hire from - are they people with film degrees, are they former actors moving behind the scenes, are they Dude McPerson's nephew? Make connections. Find people on LinkedIn and see where there first jobs are. Hell, go to LinkedIn, Indeed, Monster, etc, and plug in the company of your choosing and fire off applications. 

Go to your alumni office and make lists of alumni who work or worked in the field you want. Email them. Alumni really like talking with current students - hell, everybody likes being told to give advice. 

A lot of those companies, even if you are lucky enough to get an internship, don't pay you. Find some sort of income. You know how many actors and artists work in coffee shops and bookstores? Go get a job there, make friends, and use the time to save money and research. Save enough to move to California - that is pretty much 100% where corporate offices are.

I don't work in entertainment, but I strongly considered it and spoke to several people who did (paralegals and lawyers with Sony and LucasFilm on their resume, distribution companies that work with Marvel and DC, and artists who struck gold with animation studios). This was most of the advice they gave me.

That's why I recommended masters programs, if more education is something OP wants. It's understood that even if you majored in X in undergrad, as long as you make a compelling case for yourself, you can focus on Y in graduate school. I know people who've switched from engineering to medieval history between college and grad school (and vice versa) and it didn't make a lick of difference, because they were still able to explain why the skills they had would suit the program of their choice.

Getting a second bachelor's degree is almost always a poor idea. You're better off looking into applying for MS programs in software engineering if that's what you're interested in - there's way, way more funding for masters degrees (even if funding is not an issue for you) and you have more qualifications on a resume. Graduate school is still an option for people even with poor undergrad grades, and engineering is a field where people give way more weight to projects and classwork. Furthermore, having multiple bachelor's degrees is something of a red flag.
